On the bi-Hamiltonian structures
of the Camassa-Holm
and Harry Dym equations

Paolo Lorenzoni Affiliation: Dipartimento di Matematica e Applicazioni Affiliation: Università di Milano-Bicocca Affiliation: Via Roberto Cozzi 53, I-20125 Milano, Italy Email: lorenzoni@matapp.unimib.it Affiliation: Marco Pedroni Affiliation: Dipartimento di Matematica Affiliation: Università di Genova Affiliation: Via Dodecaneso 35, I-16146 Genova, Italy Email: pedroni@dima.unige.it
Abstract

We show that the bi-Hamiltonian structures of the Camassa-Holm and Harry Dym hierarchies can be obtained by applying a reduction process to a simple Poisson pair defined on the loop algebra of 𝔰​𝔩​(2,ℝ)\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R}). The reduction process is a bi-Hamiltonian reduction, that can be canonically performed on every bi-Hamiltonian manifold.

1 Introduction

In recent years a lot of papers have been devoted to the Camassa-Holm equation (CH)

ut−ut​x​x=−3​u​ux+2​ux​ux​x+u​ux​x​xu_{t}-u_{txx}=-3uu_{x}+2u_{x}u_{xx}+uu_{xxx} (1)

or, putting m=u−ux​xm=u-u_{xx},

mt=−2​m​ux−mx​u,m_{t}=-2mu_{x}-m_{x}u, (2)

introduced in [4] as a model of shallow water waves. Part of them [2, 3, 13, 22] have investigated the connections with the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation

ut=−3​u​ux+ux​x​x,u_{t}=-3uu_{x}+u_{xxx}, (3)

the Hunter-Saxton (HS) equation [11]

ut​x​x=−2​ux​ux​x−u​ux​x​x,u_{txx}=-2u_{x}u_{xx}-uu_{xxx}, (4)

and the Harry Dym (HD) equation

ut=(u−12)x​x​x,u_{t}=\left(u^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)_{xxx}, (5)

attributed in [14] to Harry Dym. In particular, Khesin and Misiolek [13], motivated by [2] and [3], have explained the connections between KdV, CH with linear dispersion,

ut−ut​x​x=−3​u​ux+2​ux​ux​x+u​ux​x​x+c​ux​x​x,u_{t}-u_{txx}=-3uu_{x}+2u_{x}u_{xx}+uu_{xxx}+cu_{xxx}, (6)

and HS in terms of their common symmetry group, the Virasoro group. Indeed, these equations can be interpreted as Euler equations describing the geodesic flow (with respect to different metrics): on the Virasoro group in the KdV and CH (c≠0c\neq 0) case [24, 23], on the diffeomorphism group of the circle in the CH (c=0c=0) case [23, 7], and on a suitable homogeneous space in the HS case [13]. Moreover, to any (codimension 2) coadjoint orbit there corresponds a bi-Hamiltonian structure: the first Poisson bracket is just the Lie-Poisson bracket, while the second one is a constant bracket depending on the choice of a point in the dual of the Virasoro algebra. Points on the same orbit give rise to equivalent choices. There are three types of orbit and three different associated bi-Hamiltonian structures: the KdV, the CH and the HS bi-Hamiltonian structures.

As regards the connections between CH and HD, they are clear in the framework of the inverse scattering techniques [2]. Indeed, both the equations are associated to the scattering problems for the family of operators

Lk=∂x2+k2ρ2−q.\displaystyle L_{k}=\partial_{x}^{2}+k^{2}\rho^{2}-q.

A different choice of the boundary conditions for the function ρ⁡(x)\rho(x) and of the value of the constant qq selects the associated equation: the case q=0q=0 and ρ→1\rho\rightarrow 1 at infinity corresponds to HD, while the case q=14q=\frac{1}{4} and ρ→0\rho\rightarrow 0 at infinity corresponds to CH.

In this paper we investigate the connections between CH and HD from a different point of view. More precisely, we show that the CH and HD bi-Hamiltonian structures can be obtained by a bi-Hamiltonian reduction procedure from the Poisson pencil

P(λ)=P2+λP1=∂x+[⋅,A]+λ[⋅,S],\displaystyle P_{(\lambda)}=P_{2}+\lambda P_{1}=\partial_{x}+[\cdot,A]+\lambda[\cdot,S],

defined on the space ℳ=C∞​(S1,𝔰​𝔩​(2,ℝ)){\cal M}=C^{\infty}(S^{1},\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})) of C∞C^{\infty} maps from the unit circle to the Lie algebra of 2×22\times 2 traceless matrices. SS is a point of ℳ{\cal M} and AA is an arbitrary constant traceless matrix. The reduction procedure depends on the choice of the conjugacy class of AA.

It turns out that there are three different reduced bi-Hamiltonian structures: one is the CH bi-Hamiltonian structure (rank​(A)=2\mbox{rank}(A)=2), one is the HD bi-Hamiltonian structure (rank​(A)=1\mbox{rank}(A)=1) and one, up to a change of coordinates, is still the HD bi-Hamiltonian structure (A=0A=0).

Since the HD bi-Hamiltonian structure can be obtained from HS bi-Hamiltonian structure just by a change of variables [12], and taking into account the correspondence between coadjoint Virasoro orbits and Jordan normal forms in S​L​(2,ℝ)SL(2,\mathbb{R}), we observe that this result seems to be strictly related to those of Khesin and Misiolek.

The paper is organized as follows: In section 2 we summarize some useful techniques in the theory of the bi-Hamiltonian reduction. In section 3 we formalize and prove the above mentioned results.

2 The bi-Hamiltonian reduction

In this section we recall a reduction process of the Marsden-Ratiu type [21], that can be performed on every bi-Hamiltonian manifold. It has been presented in [5] and then applied to the Drinfeld-Sokolov hierarchies [9] in [6, 25] and to the stationary reductions of KdV in [10].

Let (ℳ,P1,P2)({\cal M},P_{1},P_{2}) be a bi-Hamiltonian manifold, i.e., a manifold ℳ{\cal M} endowed with two Poisson tensors P1P_{1} and P2P_{2} that are compatible, in the sense that their sum (and hence any linear combination) is still a Poisson tensor (see, e.g., [19, 18]). Let us fix a symplectic leaf 𝒮{\cal S} of P1P_{1} and consider the distribution D=P2​(Ker​P1)D=P_{2}(\mbox{Ker}P_{1}) on ℳ{\cal M}.

Theorem 1

The distribution DD is integrable. If E=D∩T​𝒮E=D\cap T{\cal S} is the distribution induced by DD on 𝒮{\cal S} and the quotient space 𝒩=𝒮/E{\cal N}={\cal S}/E is a manifold, then it is a bi-Hamiltonian manifold.

The reduced Poisson tensors P1redP_{1}^{\mbox{\scriptsize red}} and P2redP_{2}^{\mbox{\scriptsize red}} on 𝒩{\cal N} are constructed as follows. For any point p∈𝒮p\in{\cal S} and any covector α∈Tπ⁡(p)∗​𝒩\alpha\in T^{*}_{\pi(p)}{\cal N}, where π:𝒮→𝒩\pi:{\cal S}\to{\cal N} is the canonical projection, there is a covector α~∈Tp∗​ℳ\tilde{\alpha}\in T^{*}_{p}{\cal M} such that

α~|Dp=0,α~|Tp​𝒮=πp∗​α,\tilde{\alpha}|_{D_{p}}=0\ ,\qquad\tilde{\alpha}|_{T_{p}{\cal S}}=\pi^{*}_{p}\alpha\ ,

where πp∗:Tπ⁡(p)∗​𝒩→Tp∗​𝒮\pi^{*}_{p}:T^{*}_{\pi(p)}{\cal N}\to T^{*}_{p}{\cal S} is the codifferential of π\pi at pp. Then

(Pired)π⁡(p)α=π∗p((Pi)pα~),i=1,2.\left(P_{i}^{\mbox{\scriptsize red}}\right)_{\pi(p)}\alpha={\pi_{*}}_{p}\left((P_{i})_{p}\tilde{\alpha}\right)\ ,\qquad i=1,2\ .

Whenever an explicit description of the quotient manifold 𝒩{\cal N} is not available, the following technique to compute the reduced bi-Hamiltonian structure (already employed in [6] for the Drinfeld-Sokolov case) is very useful.

Theorem 2

Suppose 𝒬{\cal Q} to be a submanifold of 𝒮{\cal S} which is transversal to the distribution EE, in the sense that

Tp​𝒬⊕Ep=Tp​𝒮for all p∈𝒬.T_{p}{\cal Q}\oplus E_{p}=T_{p}{\cal S}\qquad\mbox{for all $p\in{\cal Q}$}\ . (7)

Then 𝒬{\cal Q} (which is locally diffeomorphic to 𝒩{\cal N}) also inherits a bi-Hamiltonian structure from ℳ{\cal M}. The reduced Poisson pair on 𝒬{\cal Q} is given by

(Pird)pα=Πp((Pi)pα~),i=1,2,\left(P_{i}^{\rm{rd}}\right)_{p}\alpha=\Pi_{p}\left((P_{i})_{p}\tilde{\alpha}\right)\ ,\qquad i=1,2\ , (8)

where p∈𝒬p\in{\cal Q}, α∈Tp∗​𝒬\alpha\in T^{*}_{p}{\cal Q}, Πp:Tp​𝒮→Tp​𝒬\Pi_{p}:T_{p}{\cal S}\to T_{p}{\cal Q} is the projection relative to (7), and α~∈Tp∗​ℳ\tilde{\alpha}\in T^{*}_{p}{\cal M} satisfies

α~|Dp=0,α~|Tp​𝒬=α.\tilde{\alpha}|_{D_{p}}=0\ ,\qquad\tilde{\alpha}|_{T_{p}{\cal Q}}=\alpha\ . (9)

In the next section we will follow this procedure to construct the bi-Hamiltonian structures of Camassa-Holm and Harry Dym as suitable bi-Hamiltonian reduced structures.

3 The bi-Hamiltonian structure of CH and HD

The aim of this section is to obtain the Poisson pair of Camassa-Holm and that of Harry Dym by applying the reduction procedure we have just described to a simple class of bi-Hamiltonian structures on the loop algebra of 𝔰​𝔩​(2,ℝ)\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R}).

Let ℳ=C∞​(S1,𝔰​𝔩​(2,ℝ)){\cal M}=C^{\infty}(S^{1},\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})) be the space of C∞C^{\infty}-maps from the unit circle to the Lie algebra of traceless 2×22\times 2 real matrices. The tangent space TS​ℳT_{S}{\cal M} at S∈ℳS\in{\cal M} is obviously identified with ℳ{\cal M} itself. As far as the cotangent space is concerned, we will assume that TS∗​ℳ≃TS​ℳT^{*}_{S}{\cal M}\simeq T_{S}{\cal M} by means of the nondegenerate form

⟨V1,V2⟩=∫S1tr​(V1​(x),V2​(x))​𝑑x,V1,V2∈ℳ.\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle=\int_{S^{1}}\mbox{tr}\left(V_{1}(x),V_{2}(x)\right)\,dx\ ,\qquad V_{1},V_{2}\in{\cal M}\ .

As well-known (see, e.g., [15]), the manifold ℳ{\cal M} admits a 3-parameter family of compatible Poisson tensors given by

V↦(P(a,b,c))S​V=a​∂xV+b⁡[V,S]+c⁡[V,A],S∈ℳ,V∈TS∗​ℳ,V\mapsto\left(P_{(a,b,c)}\right)_{S}V=a\partial_{x}V+b[V,S]+c[V,A]\ ,\qquad S\in{\cal M},\hskip 14.22636ptV\in T^{*}_{S}{\cal M}\ , (10)

where a,b,c∈ℝa,b,c\in\mathbb{R} and AA is any matrix in 𝔰​𝔩​(2,ℝ)\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R}). We have the following theorems.

Theorem 3

The bi-Hamiltonian reduction process applied to the pair (P1=P(1,1,0),P2=P(0,0,1))(P_{1}=P_{(1,1,0)},P_{2}=P_{(0,0,1)}) gives rise:

- to the Poisson pair of the KdV hierarchy if A=(0010)A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix};

- to the Poisson pair of the AKNS hierarchy if A=(100−1)A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix},

for suitable choices of the symplectic leaf.

Proof: See [5] and [20]. The reduction used in the latter paper is not the one presented in Theorem 1, but it is easily shown to be equivalent.

□\Box

Theorem 4

The bi-Hamiltonian reduction process applied to the pair (P1=P(0,1,0),P2=P(1,0,1))(P_{1}=P_{(0,1,0)},P_{2}=P_{(1,0,1)}) gives rise:

- to the Poisson pair of the CH hierarchy if A=12​(0110)A=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix};

- to the Poisson pair of the HD hierarchy if A=(0010)A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix},

for suitable choices of the symplectic leaf.

Proof: Let

S=(pqr−p),A=(PQR−P),S=\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\ r&-p\end{pmatrix}\ ,\qquad A=\begin{pmatrix}P&Q\\ R&-P\end{pmatrix}\ ,

with p,q,r∈C∞​(S1,ℝ)p,q,r\in C^{\infty}(S^{1},\mathbb{R}) and P,Q,R∈ℝP,Q,R\in\mathbb{R}. Since Ker​(P1)S\mbox{Ker}\left(P_{1}\right)_{S} is spanned by SS, the symplectic leaves of P1P_{1} are the level submanifolds of detS=−p2−q​r\det S=-p^{2}-qr. Moreover, we have that

DS=(P2)S​(Ker​(P1)S)={(μ​S)x+[μ​S,A]∣μ∈C∞​(S1,ℝ)}.D_{S}=(P_{2})_{S}\left(\mbox{Ker}(P_{1})_{S}\right)=\{(\mu S)_{x}+[\mu S,A]\mid\mu\in C^{\infty}(S^{1},\mathbb{R})\}\ .

Explicitly,

DS={((μ​p)x+(R​q−Q​r)​μ(μ​q)x+2​(Q​p−P​q)​μ(μ​r)x+2​(P​r−R​p)​μ−(μ​p)x−(R​q−Q​r)​μ)∣μ∈C∞​(S1,ℝ)}.D_{S}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}(\mu p)_{x}+(Rq-Qr)\mu&(\mu q)_{x}+2(Qp-Pq)\mu\\ (\mu r)_{x}+2(Pr-Rp)\mu&-(\mu p)_{x}-(Rq-Qr)\mu\end{pmatrix}\mid\mu\in C^{\infty}(S^{1},\mathbb{R})\right\}\ .

The distribution DD is not tangent to the generic symplectic leaf of P1P_{1}, but it is easily shown to be tangent to the symplectic leaf

𝒮={(pqr−p)∣p2+qr=0,(p,q,r)≠(0,0,0)},{\cal S}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\ r&-p\end{pmatrix}\mid p^{2}+qr=0,(p,q,r)\not=(0,0,0)\right\}\ , (11)

𝒬={(0q00)∣q∈C∞(S1,ℝ),q(x)≠0∀x∈S1}{\cal Q}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}0&q\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix}\mid q\in C^{\infty}(S^{1},\mathbb{R}),q(x)\neq 0\ \forall x\in S^{1}\right\} (12)

of 𝒮{\cal S} is transversal to the distribution EE. Indeed, if S⁡(q)=(0q00)S(q)=\begin{pmatrix}0&q\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix}, then

TS⁡(q)𝒮={(p˙q˙0−p˙)∣p˙,q˙∈C∞(S1,ℝ)}≃C∞(S1,ℝ)⊕C∞(S1,ℝ),T_{S(q)}{\cal S}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}\dot{p}&\dot{q}\\ 0&-\dot{p}\end{pmatrix}\mid\dot{p},\dot{q}\in C^{\infty}(S^{1},\mathbb{R})\right\}\simeq C^{\infty}(S^{1},\mathbb{R})\oplus C^{\infty}(S^{1},\mathbb{R})\ ,

and every tangent vector in TS⁡(q)​𝒮T_{S(q)}{\cal S} admits the unique decomposition

Thus the reduced Poisson pencil is

(P(λ)rd)q​α=ΠS⁡(q)​((P(λ))S⁡(q)​α~)=[−12​R2∂x3+2Q​R+P2R2∂x+λR(2q∂x+qx)]α,\begin{split}\left(P_{(\lambda)}^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd}}\right)_{q}\alpha&=\Pi_{S(q)}\left(\left(P_{(\lambda)}\right)_{S(q)}\tilde{\alpha}\right)\\ &=\left[-\frac{1}{{2R^{2}}}\partial_{x}^{3}+2\frac{QR+P^{2}}{R^{2}}\partial_{x}+\frac{\lambda}{R}(2q\partial_{x}+q_{x})\right]\alpha\ ,\end{split}

that is to say

(P1rd)q=1R(2q∂x+qx)\displaystyle\left(P_{1}^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd}}\right)_{q}=\frac{1}{R}(2q\partial_{x}+q_{x})

mt=−2​m​ux−mx​u=P1rd​δ​H1δ​m=P2rd​δ​H2δ​m,m_{t}=-2mu_{x}-m_{x}u=P_{1}^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd}}\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta m}=P_{2}^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd}}\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta m}, (14)

(P1rd)q=2q∂x+qx\displaystyle\left(P_{1}^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd}}\right)_{q}=2q\partial_{x}+q_{x}
(P2rd)q=−12∂x3.\displaystyle\left(P_{2}^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd}}\right)_{q}=-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x}^{3}\ .

ut=(u−12)x​x​x=P1rd​δ​H1δ​u=P2rd​δ​H2δ​u,u_{t}=\left(u^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)_{xxx}=P_{1}^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd}}\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta u}=P_{2}^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd}}\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta u}, (15)

H1=18​∫u−52​ux2​𝑑x,\displaystyle H_{1}=\frac{1}{8}\int u^{-\frac{5}{2}}u_{x}^{2}dx,

Theorem 5

The bi-Hamiltonian reduction process applied to the pair (P1=P(0,1,0),P2=P(1,0,1))(P_{1}=P_{(0,1,0)},P_{2}=P_{(1,0,1)}) with A=(0000)A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix}, in the space C0∞​(ℝ,𝔰​𝔩​(2,ℝ))C^{\infty}_{0}(\mathbb{R},\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})) of rapidly decreasing C∞C^{\infty}-maps from the real line to 𝔰​𝔩​(2,ℝ)\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R}), gives rise to the Poisson pair

(−2(∂x−1px+px∂x−1),∂x),(-2\left(\partial_{x}^{-1}p_{x}+p_{x}\partial_{x}^{-1}\right),\partial_{x}), (16)

where p⁡(x)p(x) is a smooth function vanishing at infinity and

∂x−1=12(∫−∞x−∫x+∞).\partial_{x}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\int_{-\infty}^{x}-\int_{x}^{+\infty}\right).

Proof: The distribution

DS={((μ​p)x(μ​q)x(μ​r)x−(μ​p)x)∣μ∈C0∞​(ℝ,ℝ)}D_{S}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}(\mu p)_{x}&(\mu q)_{x}\\ (\mu r)_{x}&-(\mu p)_{x}\end{pmatrix}\mid\mu\in C^{\infty}_{0}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\right\}\

is still tangent to 𝒮{\cal S}. In this case the transversal submanifold is

𝒬={(p1−p2−p)∣p∈C0∞(ℝ,ℝ),p(x)≠0∀x∈ℝ}{\cal Q}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}p&1\\ -p^{2}&-p\end{pmatrix}\mid p\in C^{\infty}_{0}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}),p(x)\neq 0\ \forall x\in\mathbb{R}\right\} (17)

and the projection ΠS⁡(q):TS⁡(q)​𝒮→TS⁡(q)​𝒬\Pi_{S(q)}:T_{S(q)}{\cal S}\to T_{S(q)}{\cal Q} is given by

ΠS⁡(q):(p˙,q˙)↦(p˙−p​q˙−px​∂x−1q˙,0).\Pi_{S(q)}:(\dot{p},\dot{q})\mapsto(\dot{p}-p\dot{q}-p_{x}\partial_{x}^{-1}\dot{q},0). (18)

Following the same procedure used above it is easy to see that

(P1rd)p=−2(∂x−1px+px∂x−1)\displaystyle\left(P_{1}^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd}}\right)_{p}=-2\left(\partial_{x}^{-1}p_{x}+p_{x}\partial_{x}^{-1}\right)
(P2rd)p=∂x.\displaystyle\left(P_{2}^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd}}\right)_{p}=\partial_{x}.

Moreover, taking into account that, after a change of coordinates u′=u′​(u)u^{\prime}=u^{\prime}(u), a bivector PP transforms as

P′=(∑s≥0∂u′∂u(s)∂xs)P(∑t≥0(−∂x)t∂u′∂u(t)),P^{\prime}=\left(\sum_{s\geq 0}\frac{\partial u^{\prime}}{\partial u^{(s)}}\partial_{x}^{s}\right)P\left(\sum_{t\geq 0}(-\partial_{x})^{t}\frac{\partial u^{\prime}}{\partial u^{(t)}}\right), (19)

we obtain that, in the variable u=pxu=p_{x}, the Poisson pair (P1rd,P2rd)(P_{1}^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd}},P_{2}^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd}}) coincides with the Harry Dym bi-Hamiltonian structure.

□\Box

4 Conclusions

In this paper we have shown that the bi-Hamiltonian structures of CH and HD can be seen as reductions of suitable structures on C∞​(S1,𝔰​𝔩​(2,ℝ))C^{\infty}(S^{1},\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})). In the KdV case this is a well-known result, that can be interpreted both from the Drinfeld-Sokolov point of view and in the bi-Hamiltonian reduction scheme [25].

The results of this paper could be used to construct 2-field extensions of the CH and HD hierarchies, in the same way as Drinfeld and Sokolov construct a 2-component generalization of the KdV hierarchy. This extended hierarchy lives on a symplectic leaf of P(0,0,1)P_{(0,0,1)} and projects on the usual scalar KdV hierarchy (see [9] and [18]). Analogously, we plan to define a 2-field hierarchy on the symplectic leaf 𝒮{\cal S} of CH, whose projection on the transversal submanifold 𝒬{\cal Q} is the CH hierarchy. The “unprojected” CH equation should be compared with the 2-component generalization of CH recently introduced by Liu and Zhang [16].

A crucial point in Theorem 4 is the choice of the symplectic leaf 𝒮{\cal S}. As we have already said, this leaf is special in that the distribution DD is tangent to it. Thus, for a different leaf the reduction process is more complicated and turns out to be similar to the AKNS case. It would be interesting to construct the equations corresponding to these alternative choices.
